newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss "take note" of US search for Nazi gold.
newsitem.headline: Swiss "take note" of US search for Nazi gold.

text.p: The Swiss government has taken note of the U.S. government's plan to search its archives for information on assets looted by Nazis, saying the move is in line with its own desire to find the truth about missing Jewish wealth.

"We have taken note of the State Department's action and restate the Swiss Government also wants to do everything to assure that there is clarity over what happened," foreign ministry spokesman Hans-Ruedi Bortis said on Saturday in response to inquiries.

On Friday the U.S. State Department promised a "thorough and immediate study" of what the U.S. government at the time knew about the disbursement of Nazi assets after the Second World War and the extent of U.S. contacts with the Swiss government on the question.
On Thursday a $20 billion class action suit was filed in New York on behalf of Holocaust survivors against Swiss banks for allegedly refusing to return victims' money, jewellery and other valuables.

The moves follow recent speculation, fuelled by newly declassified U.S. wartime archives, that Switzerland could still be hoarding Nazi gold or holding millions of dollars in assets from people who perished during Hitler's reign of terror.

U.S. Republican Senator Alfonse D'Amato, chairman of the Senate Banking Committee, last month called for the State Department to investigate what he called "50 years of deception" by Switzerland over the amount of funds deposited by the Nazis.

U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said his department was responding to requests by D'Amato and the World Jewish Congress about "what the U.S. government knew about the disposition of Nazi assets at that time (and) whether or not we had diplomatic contact with the Swiss government."

Bortis from the Swiss foreign ministry noted Switzerland's lower house of parliament on September 30 approved a decree from the cabinet that called for a sweeping historical study of Swiss financial dealings with Nazi Germany and the fate of Jewish wealth deposited before, during and after World War Two.
"It is the clear position of the Swiss government that it wants to do everything to clarify what happened back then," the foreign ministry spokesman said.

The decree, which also is expected to be approved by the upper chamber, creates a commission of experts empowered to lift tight bank secrecy rules for a historical accounting of Swiss commerce with Nazi Germany, for whom Swiss gold purchases were a crucial source of funds to finance their war effort.

The commission will also review how much wealth was deposited with Swiss banks and other financial companies by Jews and other victims of Nazi persecution and whether the Swiss have done enough to identify the lost assets of those killed in the Holocaust.
Separately, an international panel set up by Swiss banks and world Jewish groups last May is searching for any lost Holocaust accounts in order to return the assets to their rightful owners.
The State Department's study of its archives is expected to last two to three months and its results would be made public.
D'Amato has also urged the United States to reopen negotiations with the Swiss on a 1946 reparation treaty.

D'Amato says newly declassified U.S. government documents showed Swiss banks, companies and the government had accepted far more Nazi assets and treasures than Swiss negotiators admitted to during the 1945-46 talks.

The Swiss, however, have rejected the idea of reopening the 1946 Washington Agreement that settled Allied claims against Switzerland for Nazi assets, including stolen gold, sold or banked in the neutral Alpine country during the war.

Under the accord, the Swiss paid 250 million Swiss francs (about $60 million at the time) in return for buying gold stolen by Nazi forces and another $121 million dollars for Nazi assets frozen in Switzerland shortly before the war's end.
